changelog.change: Initial entry — converted from CV Wound Ballistics & Blast Injury Manual: wounding physics (crush vs stretch, yaw, fragmentation), caliber/construction profiles, tissue-specific patterns, forensic range-of-fire, behind-armor blunt trauma, retained-fragment workup, and antibiotic/damage-control principles.

summary: Wounding reduces to two mechanisms — tissue crush (permanent cavity) and tissue stretch (temporary cavity) — and velocity, bullet construction, and yaw predict severity far better than caliber. Plus what the entrance wound tells you about range of fire, why an intact vest doesn't exclude internal injury, and when a retained fragment actually has to come out.
whyThisMatters: The visible wound is a floor on the injury present, not a ceiling. Reasoning from mechanism and energy — how fast the round was going, how it was built, where along the track it dumped its energy — is what drives the search for occult injury, the debridement margins the surgeon needs, and the decision to image a normal-looking vessel next to a high-energy track. Getting the mental model right changes the workup before any imaging is back.
clinicalTakeaway: Build the differential from mechanism: high-velocity rifle wounds carry temporary-cavity and fragmentation injury well beyond the visible track, especially in dense organs (liver, spleen, brain) and hollow viscera; handgun wounds are mostly permanent-crush. Examine and image for injury outside the obvious track, photograph and diagram discharge findings before cleaning (soot washes off, stippling does not), treat a reported armor hit as blunt trauma of unclear mechanism, and leave most retained fragments in place — remove only for progressive deficit, referable sepsis, lead toxicity, or an intracanal spinal fragment (T12-L4) with incomplete injury.

body.text: Wounding capacity begins with kinetic energy (KE = ½mv²) and velocity dominates — doubling mass doubles energy, doubling velocity quadruples it. What matters clinically is how much energy is deposited along the wound track, not muzzle energy. Wounding reduces to two physical mechanisms: crush (the permanent cavity, tissue destroyed by direct contact and the crushing stress field — this defines debridement margins) and stretch (the temporary cavity, radial displacement from transferred energy, collapsing back within 5-10 ms).

items: Yaw / tumble: tissue is ~800× denser than air; gyroscopic stability is overwhelmed on impact. Most rifle bullets yaw within the first few centimeters; the point of maximum yaw — not the entry point — is usually where the temporary cavity peaks.

Fragmentation multiplies the permanent cavity — multiple divergent tracks from one entry, the most tissue destruction per unit of retained energy. It needs a velocity threshold (~2,000-2,200 fps); the same round can fragment at close range and produce a simple through-and-through at distance.
Deformation (hollow/soft point expansion) increases the permanent cavity 4-6× over a non-deforming bullet of the same caliber.

Stretch injures only tissue whose elastic limit it exceeds: elastic low-density tissue (lung, skeletal muscle) recoils with little lasting injury; dense encapsulated organs (liver, spleen, kidney, brain) fracture or burst; fluid/gas-distended hollow viscera can rupture at a distance like a hydraulic ram.

body.text: The hydrostatic-shock debate (can a pressure wave injure tissue it never touches?) is genuinely unresolved — Fackler argued no, the Courtneys argue yes for high-energy rifle rounds. It does not change acute management: the same thorough exam for occult injury near a high-energy track applies either way. Most cited cavitation/penetration numbers come from 10% ordnance gelatin (the FBI protocol), which bounds plausible wounding behaviour rather than predicting any one patient's wound.
Caliber alone predicts little; velocity, construction, and barrel length matter more than bore diameter. Figures are order-of-magnitude for common factory loads.

Rapid yaw (often 7-12 cm), frequent fragmentation at the cannelure, large forward temporary cavity; fragmentation unreliable past ~150-200 yd

High retained energy at range; large temporary cavity with blunt extension into surrounding tissue planes
Buckshot: multiple simultaneous crush tracks at close range. Slug: massive permanent cavity, limited penetration depth

items: Construction: FMJ resists deformation — narrow track, relies on yaw/velocity, may exit with retained energy (military ball, by international convention against expanding projectiles). Expanding (hollow/soft point) — wider, shorter track near entry, energy dumped early. Fragmenting — multiple divergent tracks.

Barrel length is a third variable: a 5.56 round that fragments reliably from a 14.5-20″ barrel can leave a 10-11″ short-barreled rifle already below the fragmentation threshold. Cartridge + range alone does not fully predict a wound.

body.text: Range of fire is read from discharge effects around the entrance wound, and carries clinical value — contact and near-contact wounds add gas-injection and thermal injury that distant wounds do not.

rows: Soot + seared charred margin; stellate tearing over bone from gas injection; possible muzzle imprint (can mimic an exit wound)
Abrasion collar + soot + stippling. Soot is water-soluble — photograph before cleaning
Abrasion collar + stippling (tattooing), no soot. Stippling is embedded and cannot be washed off

items: Entrance wounds almost always show an abrasion collar; asymmetry points toward the muzzle direction. Wound size bears no reliable relationship to caliber.
Exit wounds are typically irregular, often larger, and lack an abrasion collar or discharge residue.
Photograph and diagram discharge findings before cleaning — soot is removable, stippling is not.

body.text: Body armor and behind-armor blunt trauma (BABT)

items: Armor that stops penetration does not stop all kinetic energy. BABT comes from rapid rear-face deformation transmitting a stress wave plus shear deformation of the body wall beneath an intact vest.

Reported injuries: rib fracture, pulmonary contusion, rarely direct cardiac injury. Systematic review found no confirmed BABT fatalities from properly rated soft armor, though severe case reports exist.

An intact vest with no penetration does not exclude significant intrathoracic or intra-abdominal injury — treat a reported high-energy hit on worn armor as blunt trauma of unclear mechanism. BABT is also a proposed thoracic transmission pathway for remote brain injury.

body.text: Imaging, retained fragments, and surgical principles

items: CT trajectory reconstruction: plot entry, retained fragments, and exit; a nonlinear or discontinuous track signals yaw, ricochet off bone, or fragmentation — search specifically for secondary bone/bullet fragments along a plausible deflected path.
e-FAST is the fastest bedside screen for hemoperitoneum, hemothorax, pneumothorax; a negative study does not exclude retroperitoneal, bowel, or delayed injury in a concerning mechanism.

Retained fragments — the reflex to remove every one is outdated. Established removal indications: progressive neurologic deterioration, sepsis referable to the fragment, lead toxicity, and (spinal) an intracanal fragment roughly T12-L4 with incomplete neurologic injury. Most others can be left in place.

MRI with retained fragments: long-standing blanket avoidance is being revised — most bullets/shot are non-ferromagnetic or too small for clinically significant RF heating, and composition can often be identified on prior CT/X-ray (or dual-energy CT). Known ferromagnetic fragments (some BBs, steel-core rounds) still warrant case-by-case radiology consult.

Tetanus: address immunization status in all penetrating ballistic/blast wounds regardless of appearance. Antibiotics for isolated low-velocity soft-tissue GSW: evidence inconclusive — decide on tissue destruction, contamination, time, location, velocity (a bullet is not sterilized by firing). Viscus involvement (bowel track): broad-spectrum coverage ~48-72 h once contamination is controlled.

Damage control surgery: in the acidotic, coagulopathic, hypothermic patient the goal shifts from definitive repair to abbreviated surgery — control hemorrhage, control contamination, pack, temporarily close, resuscitate in the ICU, planned re-look. Definitive repair in a patient still in the lethal triad is a recognized way to lose a salvageable patient on the table.
